\title{Explanation Is the Bottleneck: Measuring and Gating XAI Cost in
Co-located, Fog and Cloud Deployments of Real-Time Stress Detection}

% Author block: confirm with advisor (order, affiliation, e-mail).

\begin{abstract}
Explainable AI (XAI) is routinely attached to wearable stress classifiers,
yet the time it takes to produce an explanation is almost never measured,
and never inside a deployed real-time pipeline. We deploy a frozen
\NParams-parameter 1D-CNN trained on WESAD as a TCP client--server system
and place its server co-located with the sensor client, on a fog node and
on a cloud VM. Under an open-loop sensor client with drift-corrected clock
synchronisation, we measure latency, queuing delay, execution time,
response time, jitter, bandwidth and resource usage. On the fog node a
single region-based LIME or SHAP (GradientExplainer) explanation costs
\FogXaiMinMs--\FogXaiMaxMs\ms, i.e.\ \FogXaiOverExecLow--\FogXaiOverExecHigh$\times$
the entire server-side computation of a window without explanation.
\vtwo{Without explanation the cloud placement is \CloudOverColocNone$\times$
slower than co-location; with the most expensive explainer the gap shrinks
to \CloudOverColocShap$\times$, so explanation, not placement, determines
response time.} We therefore gate explanations on model confidence. At
$\tau=\SelThr$, measured over \SelN windows, mean response time falls from
\AlwRespMean to \SelRespMean\ms (\SelSpeedup$\times$) and single-worker
capacity grows \CapGain$\times$, while \CatchElevenEighty\% of
misclassified windows of a well-calibrated subject are still explained. A
mixture model predicts the measured mean within \ProjErr\%. The benefit is
conditional on calibration: on a second held-out subject with
\ECEFourteen expected calibration error only \CatchFourteenEighty\% of errors
are caught.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
explainable AI, fog computing, real-time systems, stress detection, LIME,
SHAP, selective explanation, latency measurement
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ======================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ======================================================================

Wearable stress detection on public datasets such as WESAD~\cite{schmidt2018}
is mature, and post-hoc explanations (LIME~\cite{ribeiro2016},
SHAP~\cite{lundberg2017}) are now a standard companion to the classifier.
Explanations are, however, evaluated almost exclusively for quality: the
Co-12 review of XAI evaluation explicitly excludes run time as a property
that does not affect explanation quality~\cite{nauta2023}, and work that
applies XAI to WESAD reports neither inference nor explanation
time~\cite{almadhor2025}. In a real-time monitoring system this omission is
not cosmetic. A new 10\,s window arrives every 5\,s; whatever the server
spends explaining one window is time it cannot spend on the next window or
on the next user.

Systems work on fog-based physiological monitoring measures exactly these
transport-level quantities---latency, queuing delay, execution time,
response time, jitter, bandwidth and resource usage---but without
explanations~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025,tuli2020healthfog}. The two
literatures have not met: XAI cost is reported without a network, and
network cost without XAI.

This paper puts both in one budget. Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item An end-to-end measurement of explanation cost inside a real TCP
client--server stress detection pipeline at three placements, using the
seven metrics of~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025}, an open-loop sensor client and
drift-corrected clock synchronisation (Sec.~\ref{sec:system}).
\item Evidence that explanation dominates the pipeline by two orders of
magnitude and \vtwo{collapses the latency differences between placements}
(Sec.~\ref{sec:res-dominates}).
\item A measured characterisation of confidence-gated selective explanation:
cost, capacity and error coverage over \SelN windows, validated against a
mixture-model projection (Sec.~\ref{sec:res-selective}).
\item The calibration condition under which gating pays off, and the
quality trade-off between four explainer operating points
(Sec.~\ref{sec:res-calib}).
\end{enumerate}

% ======================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% ======================================================================

\textbf{Fog-based physiological monitoring.} Erzurumluo\u{g}lu et
al.~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025} place emotion recognition on DREAMER on a
Raspberry~Pi~4 fog worker and report the seven metrics we adopt; their
worker answers in 43.3\ms and their cloud in 73.3\ms. HealthFog~\cite{tuli2020healthfog}
compares edge, fog and cloud placements for cardiac diagnosis in terms of
latency and energy. Neither includes explanations. El~Rashidy et
al.~\cite{elrashidy2025} combine a fog architecture with LIME and Grad-CAM
for emotion recognition but report no per-inference latency or explanation
cost.

\textbf{The cost of explanation.} ShaTS~\cite{shats2025} states the only
explicit real-time bound we found---an explainer taking more than 1\,s per
window is unsuitable for real-time use---and shows KernelSHAP violating it.
Reported costs vary by orders of magnitude with hardware, input size and
estimator: KernelSHAP takes seconds to minutes per
sample~\cite{warnecke2020,jethani2022}, whereas amortised estimators such as
FastSHAP~\cite{jethani2022} trade a long training phase for millisecond
explanations. On constrained hardware, a conditionally triggered SHAP on a
Raspberry~Pi~4 added about 195\ms per prediction~\cite{taguta2026}.

\textbf{Selective computation.} Gating computation on softmax confidence is
established for inference (early exits~\cite{teerapittayanon2017},
confidence cascades~\cite{berestizshevsky2018}) and has been proposed for
explanations: budgeted selective explanations~\cite{paes2024} and
explanations of rejected samples~\cite{artelt2023}. We do not claim the
mechanism; we characterise it end to end in continuous physiological
monitoring, where its benefit turns out to hinge on calibration~\cite{guo2017}.

\subsection{Model}
The classifier is a temporal 1D-CNN (two convolution blocks with [32,\,128]
filters, kernel 9, BatchNorm--ReLU--MaxPool--Dropout, global average
pooling, two dense layers; \NParams parameters) trained with focal
loss~\cite{lin2017} on 14 chest and wrist channels resampled to 64\,Hz, in
10\,s windows with 5\,s hop. The architecture attains 0.92~F1 under 15-fold
leave-one-subject-out validation; the deployed checkpoint was trained on 13
subjects with S11 and S14 held out (validation F1 \ValFOne). We chose it over
a transformer from our offline study that reached higher single-split
accuracy because it is 37$\times$ smaller and 29$\times$ faster per window on the
same CPU (1.86\,M parameters, 103.7 vs.\ 3.6\ms; measured
offline\todo{archive this measurement under results/}); the model is frozen and used unchanged in every measurement.

\subsection{Real-time pipeline}
The client replays a WESAD record at the sensors' native rates (chest
700\,Hz, wrist 4--64\,Hz) in 500\,ms ticks; each tick is one binary frame of
\PayloadBytes bytes. Resampling happens on the server and is part of the
measured execution time. Offline training normalised each subject with
statistics of the full record, which leaks the future; the server instead
uses causal (Welford) normalisation from data seen so far. Under this
constraint the deployed model reaches \RtAcc accuracy and \RtFOne stress F1
on \RtN labelled windows of S11 and S14---the drop is the price of
leak-free normalisation, not of the transport.

\subsection{Transport and measurement}
\label{sec:transport}
\textbf{Single worker with an explicit queue.} A reader task timestamps each
frame on arrival ($t_\mathrm{recv}$) and enqueues it; one worker drains the
queue ($t_\mathrm{start}$, $t_\mathrm{end}$). Latency $=t_\mathrm{recv}-t_\mathrm{send}$,
queuing delay $=t_\mathrm{start}-t_\mathrm{recv}$, execution $=t_\mathrm{end}-t_\mathrm{start}$,
response $=t_\mathrm{reply}-t_\mathrm{send}$; jitter is the mean absolute
change of consecutive response times, as in~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025}.
Nagle's algorithm is disabled (\texttt{TCP\_NODELAY}).

\textbf{Open-loop load.} A client that waits for each reply before sending
the next tick is a \emph{closed} load generator: when an explanation takes
longer than the 500\,ms tick, the emulated sensor stops, later ticks are sent
in a burst, and the waiting is omitted from the measurement---the
coordinated-omission problem of closed-loop benchmarking~\cite{schroeder2006}.
In a local check with the most expensive explainer, a closed-loop client
stalled the sensor stream by up to \LoopClosedLagPNF\ms (95th percentile);
our open-loop client sends every tick on its schedule from a separate task
(send-lag p95 \LoopOpenLagPNF\ms, bounded by the Windows timer). We
additionally report the \emph{sensor age} of a decision,
$t_\mathrm{reply}$ minus the scheduled send time, which is immune to
coordinated omission.

\textbf{Clocks.} One-way latency needs the client and server clocks. We use
monotonic \texttt{perf\_counter} clocks and estimate their offset NTP-style
from the minimum-RTT exchange of 12 ping rounds~\cite{mills1991}. Because
crystal drift made a single estimate yield negative latencies over 87-minute
runs, the offset is re-measured every 60\,s and interpolated linearly per
packet. The uncertainty is half the minimum RTT; where it is of the same
order as the latency itself (the cloud), we report the network share
$(\text{response}-\text{execution}-\text{queuing})/2$ instead of one-way
latency.

\subsection{Explainers and confidence gating}
\textbf{Region-based LIME.} The $14\times640$ window is divided into 20 time
segments per channel (280 regions); a masked region is replaced by the
channel mean, samples are weighted with an exponential kernel and fitted
with ridge regression. Operating points: 500 samples (\emph{LIME}) and 250
(\emph{LIME-cheap}). \textbf{\shapge.} SHAP's GradientExplainer (expected
gradients~\cite{erion2021}) with a fixed 100-window k-means background
drawn from training subjects in the causal input space; 200 samples
(\emph{SHAP}) and 50 (\emph{SHAP-cheap}). This is not KernelSHAP, whose
cost structure differs~\cite{warnecke2020}. Explainers are warmed up at
server start-up (the first \shapge call takes seconds), outside measurement.

\textbf{Gating.} Let $c$ be the maximum softmax probability. A window is
explained iff $c<\tau$; $\tau=0$ never explains and $\tau=1$ always does.

\section{Experimental Setup}
% ======================================================================

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Placements. Network share is $(\text{resp.}-\text{exec.}-\text{queue})/2$
without explanation (median).}
\label{tab:placements}
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{1.05cm}p{3.0cm}p{2.3cm}r@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Tier} & \textbf{Server hardware} & \textbf{Software stack} & \textbf{Net}\\
\midrule
Co-loc. & \ColocHW, \ColocRAM\,GB; loopback & \ColocStack & \ColocNoneNet\ms\\
Fog        & \FogHW, \FogRAM\,GB; LAN & \FogStack & \FogNoneNet\ms\\
Cloud      & \CloudHW, \CloudRAM\,GB; Internet & \CloudStack & \CloudNoneNet\ms\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Placements} (Table~\ref{tab:placements}). We use \emph{co-located}
rather than ``edge'': client and server run as separate processes on the same
machine and talk over loopback, which is the lowest-latency placement
available; it is not a wearable. The fog server is a separate device on the
local network and the cloud server a VM reached over the Internet. \vtwo{Fog and
cloud servers run the same container image and the co-located server the
same pinned versions natively (Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.14 CPU build), so the
tiers differ in hardware and network only; the fog node is a
Raspberry~Pi on Ethernet with active cooling, the performance governor and
throttling flags logged per session.}

\textbf{Protocol.} Subject S11 (held out), causal normalisation, one PyTorch
thread, 15 warm-up windows excluded. \vtwo{Each (placement, explainer) cell
is run three times in alternating order so that thermal and frequency drift
spread evenly across placements; the unit of replication is the run, and we
report the median over runs of per-run window medians and 95th percentiles.}
Resource figures are per session. Single-worker capacity is the 5\,s hop
divided by mean execution time---an upper bound that ignores network and
phase alignment of clients.

\subsection{Explanation dominates the pipeline}
\label{sec:res-dominates}
Without explanation, the fog server spends a median \FogNoneExecMed\ms per
window on resampling, normalisation and inference---\FogNoneHopPct\% of the 5\,s hop.
A single explanation costs \FogXaiMinMs to \FogXaiMaxMs\ms
(Table~\ref{tab:tiers}), \FogXaiOverExecLow--\FogXaiOverExecHigh$\times$ the
whole pipeline it explains, and response time grows
\FogRespGrowth$\times$. Explanation accounts for nearly all of the execution
time once enabled, and peak server memory more than doubles because the
explainer's background set and graph live alongside the model. Against the
1\,s/window bound of~\cite{shats2025}, both cheap operating points fit
\vtwo{on the desktop-class servers} while the full LIME and \shapge points
exceed it at the 95th percentile.

\vtwo{\textbf{Placement under explanation.} Without explanation, placement
dominates response time: the cloud is \CloudOverColocNone$\times$ slower
than co-location because its network share (\CloudNoneNet\ms) is an order
of magnitude larger than the computation. With explanation the ordering is
set by compute: cloud/co-located is \CloudOverColocShapC$\times$ for
SHAP-cheap and \CloudOverColocShap$\times$ for SHAP, because tens of
milliseconds of network vanish next to a second of explanation.}
\todo{v2: rewrite this paragraph from the Pi numbers. Expected: the Pi fog
is compute-bound, every-window explanation exceeds the 1\,s bound and may
approach the 5\,s hop, so placement matters again---through compute, not
network.} \ifvone In v1 the fog/co-located ratio of explanation time
\emph{changes sign} across explainers (\FogOverColocXaiLime for LIME,
\FogOverColocXaiShapC for SHAP-cheap), which hardware alone cannot cause;
it reflects the different PyTorch builds and is why v2 uses one image.\fi

We also observe that the network share of response time grows when
explanations are enabled on wireless and Internet paths (fog
\FogNoneNet\,$\to$\,\FogShapCNet\ms, cloud \CloudNoneNet\,$\to$\,\CloudShapCNet\ms
with SHAP-cheap) but not on loopback. \vtwo{A plausible cause is radio power
saving during the idle gap while the server explains; the Ethernet-connected
fog node in v2 separates the two.}

\subsection{Selective explanation recovers the cost}
\label{sec:res-selective}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Never / selective / always explaining on the fog node (SHAP-cheap).
Means are reported because the selective distribution is bimodal.}
\label{tab:selective}
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Policy} & \textbf{Win.} & \textbf{Expl.} & \textbf{Resp.} & \textbf{Exec.} & \textbf{Clients}\\
& & & mean (ms) & mean (ms) & per worker\\
\midrule
never ($\tau{=}0$)          & \FogNoneN & 0\%        & \NonRespMean & \NonExecMean & \CapNon\\
selective ($\tau{=}\SelThr$) & \SelN     & \SelRate\% & \SelRespMean & \SelExecMean & \CapSel\\
always ($\tau{=}1$)         & \AlwN     & 100\%      & \AlwRespMean & \AlwExecMean & \CapAlw\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

We ran the full \SelMinutes-minute S11 record on the fog node with SHAP-cheap and
$\tau=\SelThr$ (Table~\ref{tab:selective}). \SelNExpl of \SelN windows
(\SelRate\%) were explained at \SelPerExpl\ms each; mean response fell from
\AlwRespMean to \SelRespMean\ms (\SelSpeedup$\times$) and capacity rose from
\CapAlw to \CapSel clients per worker (\CapGain$\times$). The median window
is not explained (\SelRespMedian\ms) and the 95th percentile is an explained
window (\SelRespPNF\ms). The bursty load did not build a queue: the 99th
percentile queuing delay of prediction packets stayed at \SelQueueMax\ms. A
mixture model that combines the calibration-set explanation rate with the
per-explanation cost predicted the mean response within \ProjErr\% and the
explanation rate within \ProjRateErr\%, so the projections for other
explainers and thresholds can be trusted.

Short runs are misleading here: in the first five minutes of S11 the lowest
confidence was above 0.9, and no threshold triggered a single explanation.
Confidence is non-stationary within a record, so gating must be evaluated on
full records.

\subsection{The calibration condition}
\label{sec:res-calib}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Explanation rate and share of misclassified windows that are
explained, per threshold (causal input space, uncalibrated softmax).}
\label{tab:calib}
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{S11} (ECE \ECEEleven)} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{S14} (ECE \ECEFourteen)}\\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3}\cmidrule(lr){4-5}
$\tau$ & explained & errors caught & explained & errors caught\\
\midrule
0.70 & \RateElevenSeventy\% & \CatchElevenSeventy\% & \RateFourteenSeventy\% & \CatchFourteenSeventy\%\\
0.80 & \RateElevenEighty\%  & \CatchElevenEighty\%  & \RateFourteenEighty\%  & \CatchFourteenEighty\%\\
0.90 & \RateElevenNinety\%  & \CatchElevenNinety\%  & \RateFourteenNinety\%  & \CatchFourteenNinety\%\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Gating saves cost on both held-out subjects, but it only targets errors if
confidence is calibrated~\cite{guo2017}. The model is equally confident on
both subjects (mean \ConfEleven vs.\ \ConfFourteen) but correct on
\AccEleven vs.\ \AccFourteen of windows; S14 is confidently wrong
(Table~\ref{tab:calib}). At $\tau=0.80$ the explanation rate is similar
(\RateElevenEighty vs.\ \RateFourteenEighty\%), yet \CatchElevenEighty\% of
S11's errors and only \CatchFourteenEighty\% of S14's are explained.
Cross-subject temperature scaling made both worse (ECE \ECEtsEleven and
\ECEtsFourteen) because the miscalibration has opposite signs. The cost
claim and the coverage claim must therefore be stated separately: the
former holds generally, the latter requires per-user calibration.

\subsection{Explainer quality versus cost}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Explainer operating points: fog cost and quality on \QualN windows
of S11 (faithfulness = insertion$-$deletion AUC $\pm$ s.e.m.; lower
sensitivity is better).}
\label{tab:quality}
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Explainer} & \textbf{xai (ms)} & \textbf{Faithfulness} & \textbf{Monoton.} & \textbf{Sensitivity}\\
\midrule
SHAP-cheap & \FogShapCXaiMed & \FaithShapC$\pm$\FaithSemShapC & \MonoShapC & \SensShapC\\
LIME-cheap & \FogLimeCXaiMed & \FaithLimeC$\pm$\FaithSemLimeC & \MonoLimeC & \SensLimeC\\
LIME       & \FogLimeXaiMed  & \FaithLime$\pm$\FaithSemLime   & \MonoLime  & \SensLime\\
SHAP       & \FogShapXaiMed  & \FaithShap$\pm$\FaithSemShap   & \MonoShap  & \SensShap\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

No operating point dominates on faithfulness: all differences lie within one
standard error (Table~\ref{tab:quality}). The explainers separate on
stability instead: LIME is \SensRatio$\times$ less sensitive to small input
noise than \shapge, while SHAP-cheap is the cheapest point. The choice is
therefore between cost and stability, not fidelity, and the cheap points
lose nothing measurable in faithfulness.

% ======================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}
% ======================================================================

\textbf{Where the architectural decision moves.} In the reference fog
study~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025}, as in our runs without explanation, the
placement decision is a latency decision. Once explanations are produced,
the decisive parameter becomes the triggering policy: it changes mean
response time by \SelSpeedup$\times$ and capacity by \CapGain$\times$,
\vtwo{more than any placement change we measured.}

\textbf{Comparison with the reference system.} Only bandwidth is directly
comparable, because hardware and windowing differ: streaming raw
multichannel signal costs us \FogKbps\,kbps, versus 373.9\,kbps for sending
24 extracted features at 32 requests per second
in~\cite{erzurumluoglu2025}.

\textbf{Limitations.} (i) Two held-out subjects; the calibration finding is
an observation on $n=2$, not a generalisation. (ii) One worker per server;
multi-worker scheduling is future work. (iii) Capacity is an analytical
upper bound; \vtwo{multi-client open-loop runs are in progress.}
(iv) No user study of explanation usefulness. (v) This is an emulation:
recorded data replayed at native rates, not a live wearable.

% ======================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% ======================================================================

Measured end to end, explanation---not inference and \vtwo{not
placement}---is the bottleneck of real-time explainable stress detection:
it costs two orders of magnitude more than the pipeline it explains.
Confidence-gated explanation recovers most of that cost and raises
single-worker capacity \CapGain$\times$, but explains errors only where the
model is calibrated. We release the measurement harness, including the
open-loop client and drift-corrected clock synchronisation.
